title: Window Navigation Frames and Distributions
description: Detect changes with LAG, define running and moving frames, and interpret tied distributions and median edge cases without losing observation identity.

questions.question_text: What does a window calculation retain compared with ordinary grouping?
options: A value for each query row
Only one row for the whole database
questions.explanation: Window expressions do not inherently collapse the rows.

questions.question_text: What resets LAG independently for each device?
questions.explanation: Partitions define separate related populations.

questions.question_text: Why add id after a potentially tied timestamp in window ordering?
questions.explanation: A complete order resolves ties.

questions.question_text: What does LAG return at the start without an explicit default?
questions.explanation: No preceding row yields the default missing result.

questions.question_text: Why carry ROW_NUMBER for a null-aware change detector?
options: It distinguishes a first row from a null predecessor
questions.explanation: Both situations can otherwise show a null LAG value.

questions.question_text: Where should a MySQL query filter a calculated LAG result?
options: The same block WHERE using the window expression
An outer query over a CTE or derived result
questions.explanation: Window evaluation follows the same-block WHERE phase.

questions.question_text: Which explicit frame gives a positional running total?
options: ROWS BETWEEN CURRENT ROW AND CURRENT ROW
ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
questions.explanation: The frame grows from the partition start to this row.

questions.question_text: What can the default ordered RANGE frame do with tied ordering values?
options: Raise an error for every tie
Choose only the lowest identifier automatically
questions.explanation: Range peers share ordering values.

questions.question_text: Does a three-row moving frame always mean three minutes?
questions.explanation: Row counts and elapsed time are different frame models.

questions.question_text: How does AVG treat NULL values within a frame?
options: It excludes them from its known-value denominator
questions.explanation: A missing observation is not automatically a zero value.

questions.question_text: What is PERCENT_RANK for a singleton partition?
questions.explanation: The singleton boundary has defined zero percent rank.

questions.question_text: For sorted 10, 20, 20, 40, what is CUME_DIST at either 20?
questions.explanation: Three of four rows are at or below that peer group.

questions.question_text: Do distribution position functions directly return an interpolated median value?
questions.explanation: They assign positions to existing rows.

questions.question_text: Under the middle-values rule, what is the median of 10 and 40?
questions.explanation: Average the two middle values.

questions.question_text: Why retain duplicate numeric values in a median population?
options: Every duplicate is a data error
They force the median to NULL
questions.explanation: Deduplicating values changes statistical weighting.

questions.question_text: What does LAST_VALUE refer to for a frame-sensitive calculation?
options: Always the final row of the entire table
The greatest identifier regardless of order
The last row of its frame
questions.explanation: The frame boundary controls the value.

questions.question_text: Does adding a frame make LAG behave like a framed SUM?
questions.explanation: Navigation and aggregate frame semantics differ.

questions.question_text: What should a global median over no known values return under the shown AVG approach?
questions.explanation: No middle observations leave an empty aggregate population.

questions.question_text: For device values 10, 15, 12, what are positional running totals?
questions.explanation: Each row adds its known value to the prior cumulative sum.

questions.question_text: Which transition is detected by NOT(value <=> prev) after the first row?
options: A known value changing to NULL
questions.explanation: Null-safe equality distinguishes known-to-missing changes.

coding_problems.title: Compute device running totals
coding_problems.task: Return id, running_total for each reading. Partition by device_id, order by observed_at then id, and use an explicit positional frame from partition start through current row. Order final output by id.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE readings(id INT PRIMARY KEY,device_id INT NOT NULL,observed_at DATETIME NOT NULL,value INT NULL);
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT id,SUM(value) OVER(PARTITION BY device_id ORDER BY observed_at,id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS running_total FROM readings ORDER BY id;
coding_problems.ordering: Final id ascending; window sequence uses timestamp then id.
coding_problems.explanation: Each partition accumulates in a complete deterministic sequence.

coding_problems.title: Find null-aware device changes
coding_problems.task: Return id for nonfirst readings whose value differs from the preceding reading of the same device. Order within devices by observed_at, id. Treat two NULLs as equal and one NULL versus known as different. Order result by id.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE readings(id INT PRIMARY KEY,device_id INT NOT NULL,observed_at DATETIME NOT NULL,value INT NULL);
coding_problems.solution_sql: WITH compared AS(SELECT id,value,ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY device_id ORDER BY observed_at,id) AS rn,LAG(value) OVER(PARTITION BY device_id ORDER BY observed_at,id) AS prev FROM readings) SELECT id FROM compared WHERE rn>1 AND NOT(value <=> prev) ORDER BY id;
hints: Carry row position as well as LAG.
coding_problems.explanation: The outer filter separates first-row status from predecessor missingness and detects real value transitions.

notes:
## Keep each observation while comparing related rows

A window function calculates across a related set of query rows while retaining an output value for each row. This makes it useful for campus equipment readings, enrollment changes, and financial activity reports. An ordinary GROUP BY collapses observations to group rows; a window expression can instead show each observation alongside its previous value, cumulative total, or relative distribution position.

Three separate choices define a window calculation: partition membership, ordering, and sometimes a frame. Partitioning resets the calculation for each device or account. Ordering defines which observation precedes another. A frame selects the subset used by frame-sensitive functions at the current row. State these choices explicitly before interpreting any number, especially when timestamps can repeat or observations can be missing.

## Navigate with LAG and LEAD

LAG retrieves an earlier row's expression in the ordered partition, while LEAD retrieves a later row's expression. A missing neighboring row normally yields null unless an explicit supported default is supplied. A null value stored in an existing neighbor is still missing information; it is not automatically the same situation as reaching a partition boundary.

```sql
CREATE TABLE readings(id INT PRIMARY KEY,device_id INT NOT NULL,
 observed_at DATETIME NOT NULL,value INT NULL);
INSERT INTO readings VALUES
 (1,7,'2026-10-01 09:00:00',10),(2,7,'2026-10-01 09:01:00',15),
 (3,7,'2026-10-01 09:01:00',12),(4,8,'2026-10-01 09:00:00',20);
SELECT id,device_id,value,
 LAG(value) OVER(PARTITION BY device_id ORDER BY observed_at,id) AS previous_value
FROM readings ORDER BY device_id,observed_at,id;
```

Device 7 receives previous values null, 10, and 15. Device 8 begins a new partition and receives null. The identifier breaks the timestamp tie for readings 2 and 3. Without a complete ordering, previous value is ambiguous for tied observations, so a change detector could produce unstable transitions even when the stored measurements remain unchanged.

## Detect change with a second query stage

Window results cannot generally be referenced directly in the same query block's WHERE clause in MySQL. Calculate previous values in a CTE or derived relation and filter in an outer query. Decide whether the first row should count as a change, and how a transition between a known value and null should behave. Those policies belong to the application rather than to an arbitrary comparison operator.

For a null-aware change report, carry ROW_NUMBER alongside LAG. The row number distinguishes the first observation from a later observation whose predecessor value is null. MySQL's null-safe equality can compare two values as equal when both are null. Negating that equality identifies a transition where the values differ, including a known-to-null or null-to-known transition.

```sql
WITH compared AS (
 SELECT id,device_id,value,
 ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY device_id ORDER BY observed_at,id) AS rn,
 LAG(value) OVER(PARTITION BY device_id ORDER BY observed_at,id) AS prev
 FROM readings
)
SELECT id FROM compared WHERE rn>1 AND NOT(value <=> prev) ORDER BY id;
```

For the fixture, identifiers 2 and 3 are changes and the first reading of each device is excluded. If a later reading repeats the same value, it is not a change. This is different from ordinary value<>prev, which produces unknown when either value is null and can silently omit meaningful transitions.

## Make cumulative frames explicit

A running total commonly uses ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW with a deterministic order. It adds observations one position at a time. The default frame for an ordered window is range based in MySQL, which includes peers sharing the ordering value. If the order contains only a tied timestamp, several rows can receive the same cumulative total because they belong to the same peer group.

```sql
SELECT id,device_id,
 SUM(value) OVER(PARTITION BY device_id ORDER BY observed_at,id
 ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS running_total
FROM readings ORDER BY device_id,observed_at,id;
```

Device 7 totals are 10, 25, and 37; device 8 starts again at 20. SUM ignores null input values and returns null for an all-null frame. If the report requires a displayed zero for such a frame, apply that presentation rule deliberately. Do not assume that ignoring nulls means missing measurements are scientifically equivalent to measured zero.

## Moving rows and moving time are different

A three observation moving average uses ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW. At the partition start it uses the available one or two observations rather than inventing earlier rows. AVG ignores null values, so its denominator can be smaller than the number of frame positions. If the requirement demands three known observations, calculate a corresponding known-value count and suppress incomplete averages explicitly.

A preceding ten minute window asks a different question. It is based on time distance rather than the number of stored observations. Irregular sampling can make a three row frame span seconds in one period and hours in another. MySQL supports appropriate temporal RANGE frames, but the ordering and interval syntax have restrictions. Choose the frame from the business time model rather than converting a duration into an assumed fixed row count.

## Distribution positions are not interpolated percentiles

PERCENT_RANK uses rank minus one divided by partition size minus one, with zero for a singleton partition. CUME_DIST describes the fraction of rows at or below the current peer group's ordering position. For sorted values 10, 20, 20, and 40, percent ranks are 0, one third, one third, and 1; cumulative distributions are one quarter, three quarters, three quarters, and 1.

These functions assign positions to existing rows. They do not directly return an interpolated fiftieth percentile value. MySQL 8.4 does not offer the same ordered-set percentile syntax available in some other engines. For a median exercise, number nonnull values in sorted order, count the population, and average the middle one or two rows. Define the interpolation rule before comparing results across databases.

## Worked exercise: an exact median

For observations 10, 20, 20, and 40, the median under the middle-values rule is 20. For 10 and 40, it is 25. Filter null observations before numbering when the requirement defines the population as known values. A completely missing population then has no middle rows and the outer AVG returns null. This is a meaningful absence, not a zero measurement.

```sql
WITH ordered AS (
 SELECT value,ROW_NUMBER() OVER(ORDER BY value,id) AS rn,
 COUNT(*) OVER() AS n FROM readings WHERE value IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT AVG(value) AS median_value FROM ordered
WHERE rn IN ((n+1) DIV 2,(n+2) DIV 2);
```

This example computes a global median across known readings. Add partitioning and carry device identity when the requirement instead asks for one median per device. Sorting duplicates with id supplies stable row positions, while equal numeric values remain separate observations and contribute to the population count. Deduplicating values would answer a different statistical question.

## Worked exercise: interpret frame-sensitive boundaries

Compare a running sum ordered only by timestamp under the default frame with the explicit ROWS query ordered by timestamp and id. Explain why tied timestamp peers can move together in the first query and individually in the second. Then compare LAST_VALUE under a current-row-ending frame with a frame extending through the partition end. The word last refers to the frame for that function, not automatically the final observation in the partition.

LAG and LEAD navigate the partition ordering rather than shrinking their behavior to an aggregate frame. Do not assume that attaching the same frame text makes every window function use it identically. Read the function's actual contract, test singleton and tied partitions, and preserve final output ordering separately from the window's internal ordering.

## Separate population filters from display filters

A WHERE condition in the inner query changes which observations enter the windows. Filtering to today's readings before LAG means the first displayed reading cannot see yesterday's predecessor. If the requirement needs that predecessor while displaying only today, calculate navigation over a population that includes the necessary earlier observation and apply the display restriction outside. Similar care applies to running balances: removing earlier transactions before summing resets the apparent balance.

This is not a universal instruction to process all historical data. Define the required lookback and opening state for the report. A daily balance can begin with an authoritative opening balance rather than recomputing every past transaction. The essential requirement is that the window population contains enough information for the intended calculation. A query can return perfectly plausible numbers while answering a subtly narrower time interval than the user requested.

## Review and related study

Keep tests for a first observation, repeated values, repeated timestamps, null transitions, a singleton partition, and an all-null population. These cases challenge different mechanisms and should not be replaced by one long happy path. Continue with [Window Functions Ranking and Frames](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/window-functions-ranking-and-frames), [CTE Hierarchy Safety and Plans](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/cte-hierarchy-safety-and-plans), and [Selectivity](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/selectivity). Structural validation of this authored package is separate from exact engine execution and provider verification.
